props.title: La León

sections.content: La León (2007) stands as a masterpiece of slow cinema from Argentina, shot in stunning black and white by director Santiago Otheguy. The film explores isolation and sexuality along the Paraná Delta, where Alvaro, a gay man, works as a reed cutter while facing hostility from the boat captain El Turu. Its minimalist style recalls the meditative pacing of Taste of Cherry (1997) and The Turin Horse (2011), using long takes and natural sounds to create an immersive atmosphere. The waterways become both literal and metaphorical borders, reflecting themes of marginalization.

sections.content: The film's examination of masculinity in rural Latin America connects to a broader tradition of queer cinema from the region, including Wild Dogs (2004) and Bad Hair (2013). These films share an interest in how traditional machismo culture clashes with individual identity. Otheguy's decision to shoot in black and white emphasizes the stark social divisions while giving the delta landscape an otherworldly quality reminiscent of Los Muertos (2004).

Water as a cinematic metaphor reaches new depths in La León, joining films like The River (1997) and Alamar (2009) in using natural environments to explore human relationships. The Paraná Delta becomes a character itself, its labyrinthine channels reflecting Alvaro's complicated navigation of identity and belonging. SUBHEAD: Latin American Queer Cinema Movement

sections.content: La León emerged during a significant wave of Latin American LGBTQ+ cinema, alongside works like Strawberry and Chocolate (1993) and The Last Match (2013). This movement challenged traditional narratives while maintaining strong connections to regional storytelling traditions and landscapes. The film's aesthetic restraint and focus on rural life marked a departure from urban-centered queer narratives.
